text: Sorry, could you say that again?
when: When you missed what someone said
example: Sorry, could you say that again? I didn't catch the last part.

hindi.dev: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप दोबारा बोल सकते हैं?
hindi.roman: Maaf kijiye, kya aap dobara bol sakte hain?

hindi_example.dev: माफ़ कीजिए, क्या आप दोबारा बोल सकते हैं? आख़िरी हिस्सा मैं सुन नहीं पाया।
hindi_example.roman: Maaf kijiye, kya aap dobara bol sakte hain? Aakhri hissa main sun nahi paaya.

watch_out.right: Sorry, could you say that again?

gap.q: You didn't hear the teacher. Say: "Sorry, could you say that ___?"

hi_pron: सॉरी, कुड यू से दैट अगेन?
stress: sorry, could you say that aGAIN?
pron_tip: Say it in one breath; only "again" is stressed, "could you" is quick and soft.
not_when: In an email or chat; write "Could you clarify…?" instead.
memory: "Sorry" first, then the request: the sorry makes it polite.
simple: A polite way to ask someone to repeat what they just said.
more_examples: Sorry, could you say that again? The line is bad.
Sorry, could you say that again? You spoke a bit fast.
forms: Could you say that again, please? · Say that again?

confusing.diff: "Pardon?" is short and formal; "Come again?" is very casual.

real_life.everyday: The teacher speaks fast, so you ask, "Sorry, could you say that again?"
real_life.work: On a call: "Sorry, could you say that again? The network is breaking."
real_life.casual: "Sorry, could you say that again? It's really noisy here."

conversation: A: The meeting has moved to four.
B: Sorry, could you say that again?
A: Sure. The meeting is at four now.
speaking_task: You're on a phone call and the line is bad. Use this chunk, then finish the call in 2–3 lines.

when: When you greet a friend or colleague
example: Hi Ravi, how's it going?

hindi_example.dev: हाय रवि, कैसा चल रहा है?
hindi_example.roman: Hi Ravi, kaisa chal raha hai?

watch_out.why: The question needs "is" before "it": how's = how is.

gap.q: Hi Ravi, how's it ___?

not_when: With a senior officer in a formal meeting; say "How are you?"
memory: Life is a road: you ask how it is "going".
simple: A friendly way to ask "How are you?"
more_examples: How's it going with the new job?
forms: How's everything going? · How are things?
similar: How are you doing? · What's up?

confusing.pair: How's it going? vs How are you going?
confusing.diff: "How's it going?" is natural; "How are you going?" sounds odd in Indian and US English.

real_life.everyday: You meet a neighbour at the gate: "Hi, how's it going?"
real_life.work: A colleague walks in: "Morning! How's it going?"

conversation: A: Hi Ravi, how's it going?
speaking_task: Greet a friend you haven't seen for a week and ask about their new job in 2–3 lines.

when: When you meet someone for the first time
example: I'm Sana. Nice to meet you.

hindi_example.dev: मैं सना हूँ। आपसे मिलकर अच्छा लगा।
hindi_example.roman: Main Sana hoon. Aapse milkar achha laga.

watch_out.why: After "to" use the base verb, not -ing.

gap.q: I'm Sana. Nice to ___ you.

not_when: When you already know the person; say "Nice to see you."
memory: First time = MEET; next time = SEE.
simple: Said when you meet a person for the first time.
more_examples: Hi, I'm Arjun. Nice to meet you.
Nice to meet you, Mrs Rao.
forms: It's nice to meet you. · Pleased to meet you.
similar: Glad to meet you. · Pleasure to meet you.

confusing.pair: Nice to meet you vs Nice to see you
confusing.diff: "Meet" is for the first time; "see" is for people you already know.

real_life.everyday: At a wedding: "I'm Priya's cousin. Nice to meet you."
real_life.work: Meeting a new client: "Good morning. Nice to meet you."
real_life.casual: "Hey, I'm Sam. Nice to meet you!"

conversation: B: Hi Sana, I'm Karan. Nice to meet you.
A: Nice to meet you too.
speaking_task: Introduce yourself to a new classmate: your name, where you're from, and one hobby.

example: So, what do you do? I'm a nurse.

hindi_example.dev: तो, आप क्या काम करते हैं? मैं नर्स हूँ।
hindi_example.roman: Toh, aap kya kaam karte hain? Main nurse hoon.

watch_out.tip: Means 'What is your job?', not 'What are you doing now?'

gap.q: You want to know someone's job. Ask: "What do you ___?"

pron_tip: Say "what do you" fast; stress only the last "do".
not_when: When the person has just said they're a student; ask "What do you study?"
simple: A common way to ask what someone's job is.
more_examples: What do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
So, what do you do in Pune?
pattern: What do you do (for a living)?
forms: What do you do for a living? · What's your job?
similar: What line of work are you in?
reply: I'm a teacher. / I work in sales.

confusing.pair: What do you do? vs What are you doing?
confusing.diff: "What do you do?" = your job; "What are you doing?" = right now.

real_life.everyday: At a relative's house: "So, what do you do?" "I'm an engineer."
real_life.work: At a networking event: "Hi, I'm Rohan. What do you do?"
real_life.casual: "What do you do, by the way?"

conversation: A: So, what do you do?
B: I'm a nurse at City Hospital.
A: Oh, that's a tough job!
speaking_task: Answer "What do you do?" about your job or studies in 2–3 sentences, then ask it back.

when: Replying to thanks or a request
example: "Thanks for waiting." "No problem."

hindi_example.dev: "रुकने के लिए धन्यवाद।" "कोई बात नहीं।"
hindi_example.roman: "Rukne ke liye dhanyavaad." "Koi baat nahi."

gap.q: "Thanks for waiting." "No ___."

not_when: In a very formal letter; write "You're most welcome."
memory: No problem = it was easy for me.
simple: A friendly reply to "thanks" or "sorry"; it means it was fine.
forms: No problem at all. · Not a problem.
dont_say: No issues. (as a reply to thanks)

confusing.diff: Both answer "thanks"; "No problem" is more casual.

real_life.everyday: A friend thanks you for a lift: "No problem."
real_life.work: Your manager asks for a report by 5: "No problem, I'll send it."

speaking_task: Someone thanks you for helping carry books. Reply with this chunk and add one friendly line.

example: "Thank you for the help." "You're welcome."

hindi.dev: आपका स्वागत है। / कोई बात नहीं।
hindi.roman: Aapka swagat hai. / Koi baat nahi.

hindi_example.dev: "मदद के लिए धन्यवाद।" "कोई बात नहीं।"
hindi_example.roman: "Madad ke liye dhanyavaad." "Koi baat nahi."

watch_out.why: "Welcome" alone greets a guest; to answer thanks add "You're".

gap.q: "Thank you!" "You're ___."

not_when: As a welcome greeting at the door; say "Welcome!"
memory: Thank you → You're welcome: a pair.
simple: The usual polite reply when someone thanks you.
forms: You're very welcome. · You're most welcome.

confusing.diff: "You're welcome" answers thanks; "Welcome" greets someone arriving.

real_life.everyday: A child thanks you for a toffee: "You're welcome."
real_life.work: A customer thanks you at the counter: "You're welcome. Have a nice day."

conversation: A: Thank you for the help.
speaking_task: Act out helping someone at a railway station and reply to their thanks politely.

example: Good luck for your interview tomorrow!

hindi_example.dev: कल के इंटरव्यू के लिए शुभकामनाएँ!
hindi_example.roman: Kal ke interview ke liye shubhkaamnaayein!

watch_out.wrong: Good luck for your result. (after the exam)
watch_out.why: "Good luck" is before; after, you congratulate.

gap.q: Your friend has an interview today. Say: "Good ___!"

pron_tip: Don't say two d's; "good luck" sounds like one word.
not_when: After the event is over; say "Well done!" or "Congratulations!"
memory: Luck is for BEFORE; congratulations for AFTER.
simple: Said to wish someone success before something difficult.
more_examples: Good luck, we're all praying for you.
forms: Best of luck! · Good luck with that!

confusing.pair: Good luck vs All the best
confusing.diff: Both wish success; "All the best" also works as a goodbye.

real_life.everyday: Your sister leaves for her exam: "Good luck! You'll do great."
real_life.work: A colleague has a big presentation: "Good luck today!"

conversation: B: Good luck! You'll do great.
speaking_task: Wish a friend good luck before their driving test and give one piece of advice.

example: Okay, see you on Monday. Take care.

hindi_example.dev: ठीक है, सोमवार को मिलते हैं। अपना ख़्याल रखना।
hindi_example.roman: Theek hai, Somvaar ko milte hain. Apna khayal rakhna.

gap.q: Ending a call: "Bye, take ___."

not_when: When you are warning someone; say "Be careful!"
simple: A warm way to say goodbye.
more_examples: Take care of yourself, and call me.
forms: Take care of yourself. · Take good care.

confusing.diff: "Take care" is goodbye; "Be careful" warns about danger.

real_life.everyday: Ending a call with your mother: "Okay, take care. Bye."
real_life.work: Leaving the office: "See you Monday. Take care."

conversation: A: Okay, see you on Monday.
speaking_task: End a phone call with a friend who is unwell using this chunk and one more caring line.

example: "Happy Diwali!" "Same to you!"

hindi_example.dev: "दिवाली मुबारक!" "आपको भी!"
hindi_example.roman: "Diwali mubarak!" "Aapko bhi!"

gap.q: "Happy Diwali!" "Same ___ you."

not_when: When someone insults you; it sounds like a fight.
memory: Return the wish: same back to you.
simple: A reply that gives the same good wish back.
forms: And the same to you! · You too!

confusing.pair: Same to you vs You too
confusing.diff: Both return a wish; "You too" is more common for "Have a nice day".

real_life.everyday: Your neighbour says "Happy Diwali!": "Same to you!"
real_life.work: A client says "Enjoy the weekend": "Same to you!"

conversation: A: Come over for sweets later.
speaking_task: Reply to three festival wishes from different people using this chunk and "You too".

when: When you want something to be true but aren't sure
example: "Will it be sunny tomorrow?" "I hope so."

hindi_example.dev: "क्या कल धूप होगी?" "उम्मीद तो है।"
hindi_example.roman: "Kya kal dhoop hogi?" "Ummeed toh hai."

gap.q: "Will it be sunny tomorrow?" "I hope ___."

pron_tip: Stress "hope", with the voice going up a little.
not_when: When you are certain; say "Yes, definitely."
memory: Hope = I want it but I'm not sure.
simple: Means "I want that to happen, and it might."
more_examples: "Is the train on time?" "I hope so."
pattern: I hope so. / I hope not.
forms: I really hope so. · I hope not.
dont_say: I am hoping. (alone as a reply)

confusing.pair: I hope so vs I think so
confusing.diff: "Hope" = you want it; "think" = you believe it.

real_life.everyday: "Will Mum like the gift?" "I hope so."
real_life.work: "Will the client sign today?" "I hope so."
real_life.casual: "Rain tomorrow? I hope so, it's so hot!"

conversation: A: Will it be sunny tomorrow?
A: Me too, we have a picnic.
speaking_task: Answer three questions about next week with "I hope so" or "I hope not" and say why.

when: When you believe the answer is no
example: "Is the shop open?" "I don't think so."

hindi_example.dev: "क्या दुकान खुली है?" "मुझे नहीं लगता।"
hindi_example.roman: "Kya dukaan khuli hai?" "Mujhe nahi lagta."

gap.q: "Is the shop open?" "I don't think ___."

not_when: When you are sure it's no; just say "No."
simple: A polite way to say "probably not."
more_examples: "Is it going to rain?" "I don't think so."
"Did I leave the gas on?" "I don't think so."
forms: I don't think so, no. · I doubt it.

confusing.pair: I don't think so vs I think not
confusing.diff: "I think not" is very formal; use "I don't think so".

real_life.everyday: "Is the shop open on Sunday?" "I don't think so."
real_life.work: "Is the report due today?" "I don't think so. It's Friday."
real_life.casual: "Is he coming? I don't think so."

conversation: B: I don't think so. It closes at nine.
speaking_task: Politely disagree with a friend's plan using this chunk and give a reason.

when: When something hasn't happened but will
example: "Have you eaten?" "Not yet."

hindi_example.roman: "Khaana kha liya?" "Abhi nahi."

watch_out.why: "Not yet" is the natural short reply.

gap.q: "Have you eaten?" "Not ___."

pron_tip: Stress "yet"; the t of "not" is soft.
not_when: For something that will never happen; say "No."
simple: Means "no, but it will happen later."
more_examples: "Have you finished?" "Not yet, five more minutes."
forms: I haven't … yet. · Not just yet.
reply: Okay, tell me when you're done.

confusing.diff: "Not yet" = expected later; "still not" shows you're annoyed.

speaking_task: Answer questions about your to-do list using "not yet" and say when you'll do each thing.

example: "Can I use your phone?" "Sure, go ahead."

hindi_example.dev: "क्या मैं आपका फ़ोन इस्तेमाल कर सकता हूँ?" "हाँ, ज़रूर।"
hindi_example.roman: "Kya main aapka phone istemaal kar sakta hoon?" "Haan, zaroor."

watch_out.why: "Go ahead" means continue; "go" alone means leave.

gap.q: "Can I use your phone?" "Sure, go ___."

not_when: When you actually mind; say "Actually, I'd rather you didn't."
memory: Go ahead = the road is open.
simple: A friendly way to give permission.
more_examples: "May I ask a question?" "Sure, go ahead."

confusing.diff: "Go ahead" gives permission; "Go on" asks someone to continue.

real_life.everyday: "Can I use your charger?" "Sure, go ahead."
real_life.work: "Can I share my screen?" "Sure, go ahead."

conversation: A: Can I use your phone?
A: Thanks, it's just one call.
speaking_task: Three people ask you for small favours. Give permission to each using this chunk and its other forms.

when: When you suggest doing something together
example: Let's meet at six.

hindi_example.dev: चलो चलते हैं।
hindi_example.roman: Chalo chalte hain.

gap.q: Let's ___ (meet) at six.

not_when: For orders to one person; say "Please…".
memory: Let's = let us, all of us together.
simple: Used to suggest that we do something together.
pattern: Let's + base verb. / Let's not + verb.
conversation: B: Let's meet at six and go for a walk.
speaking_task: Make three suggestions for the weekend starting with "Let's".

when: When something is necessary for you
example: I need to buy a new phone.

hindi_example.dev: मुझे आराम करने की ज़रूरत है।
hindi_example.roman: Mujhe aaraam karne ki zaroorat hai.

gap.q: I need ___ (buy) a new phone.

not_when: For a rule someone else sets; "I have to" fits better.
simple: Used to say that something is necessary.
more_examples: I need to call my mom.
I need to finish this by five.
forms: I don't need to… · Do you need to…?

confusing.diff: Both mean necessary; "have to" often means a rule.

real_life.work: "I need to send this email first."

conversation: B: No, I need to buy a new phone.
speaking_task: Say three things you need to do this week and why.

when: When you ask for help with a task or thing
example: Can you help me with this bag?

hindi.dev: क्या आप … में मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?
hindi.roman: Kya aap ___ mein meri madad kar sakte hain?

hindi_example.dev: क्या आप यह बैग उठाने में मेरी मदद कर सकते हैं?
hindi_example.roman: Kya aap yeh bag uthaane mein meri madad kar sakte hain?

watch_out.wrong: Can you help me in this?
watch_out.right: Can you help me with this?

gap.q: Can you help me ___ this bag?

not_when: For big favours from seniors; "Could you…" is softer.
simple: A common way to ask for help with something.
more_examples: Can you help me with my homework?
Can you help me with this form?
pattern: Can you help me with + noun?
forms: Could you help me with…? · Can you help me (to) + verb?
similar: Could you give me a hand with…?

confusing.diff: We help someone WITH a task.

real_life.everyday: "Can you help me with these bags?"
real_life.work: "Can you help me with this Excel sheet?"
real_life.casual: "Can you help me with my resume, yaar?"

conversation: A: Can you help me with this bag?
speaking_task: Ask three people for help with three different things using this chunk.

example: What time does the shop open?

hindi_example.dev: बैंक कितने बजे खुलता है?
hindi_example.roman: Bank kitne baje khulta hai?

gap.q: What time ___ the shop open?

not_when: For a person's plan; "What time are you…?"
simple: Used to ask when something happens.
more_examples: What time does the film start?
What time does the train leave?
pattern: What time does + noun + base verb?
forms: What time do…? · What time is…?

confusing.pair: What time does vs What time is

conversation: A: What time does the shop open?
speaking_task: Ask about three timings: a bus, a shop, and a class.

example: How much are these shoes?

hindi.dev: … कितने का है / कितने के हैं?
hindi.roman: ___ kitne ka hai / kitne ke hain?

hindi_example.dev: ये जूते कितने के हैं?
hindi_example.roman: Ye joote kitne ke hain?

gap.q: How much ___ these shoes?

memory: IS for one, ARE for many.
simple: Used to ask the price of something.
pattern: How much is + singular? / How much are + plural?

confusing.diff: "Much" for price or uncountable; "many" for things you count.

real_life.everyday: At a market: "How much are these tomatoes?"

conversation: A: How much are these shoes?
A: Can you give a discount?
speaking_task: Shop for three things and ask their prices, one singular and two plural.

when: When you look for a place to do something
example: Where can I buy a SIM card?

hindi_example.dev: मैं सिम कार्ड कहाँ ख़रीद सकता हूँ?
hindi_example.roman: Main SIM card kahan khareed sakta hoon?

gap.q: Put in order (I / can / where): "___ buy a SIM card?"

not_when: For permission, not place; say "Can I…?"
simple: Used to ask where you can do or get something.
more_examples: Where can I charge my phone?
Where can I find a taxi?
forms: Where could I…? · Where do I…?
reply: There's a shop near the gate.

confusing.pair: Where can I vs Where I can

real_life.casual: "Where can I get good momos here?"

conversation: A: Where can I buy a SIM card?
speaking_task: You're new in a city. Ask three "Where can I…?" questions.

example: I think this plan is good.

hindi_example.dev: मुझे लगता है कि वह सही है।
hindi_example.roman: Mujhe lagta hai ki woh sahi hai.

watch_out.wrong: I am thinking he is right

gap.q: Give your opinion: "I ___ this plan is good."

simple: Used to give your opinion.
forms: I don't think… · Do you think…?

confusing.pair: I think vs I am thinking
confusing.diff: "I think" = opinion; "I am thinking" = in the process of thinking.

real_life.everyday: "I think the blue one is better."

conversation: B: I think this plan is good.
speaking_task: Give your opinion on three topics starting with "I think".

example: Could I borrow a pen?

hindi_example.dev: क्या मैं एक पेन ले सकता हूँ?
hindi_example.roman: Kya main ek pen le sakta hoon?

watch_out.tip: Too direct: "Give me a pen."

gap.q: Ask politely: "___ I borrow a pen?"

not_when: With a close friend it can sound too formal.
simple: A polite way to ask permission.
similar: May I…? · Would it be okay if I…?
conversation: A: Could I borrow a pen?
speaking_task: Ask your teacher for three things politely using "Could I…?".

example: Would you like some tea?

hindi_example.dev: क्या आप चाय लेंगे?
hindi_example.roman: Kya aap chai lenge?

watch_out.tip: Too direct: "Take tea."

gap.q: Would you ___ some tea?

not_when: To ask about general likes; use "Do you like…?".
simple: A polite way to offer something.
more_examples: Would you like to come with us?
pattern: Would you like + noun / to + verb?

confusing.pair: Would you like vs Do you like
confusing.diff: "Would you like" = offer now; "Do you like" = in general.

real_life.work: "Would you like to join the call?"

conversation: A: Would you like some tea?
speaking_task: Offer three things to a guest at your home.

when: When you talk about preparing to go out
example: I get ready in ten minutes.

hindi_example.dev: मैं दस मिनट में तैयार हो जाता हूँ।
hindi_example.roman: Main das minute mein taiyaar ho jaata hoon.

gap.q: I ___ ready in ten minutes.

memory: Get = become; get ready = become ready.
simple: To prepare yourself, usually to go somewhere.
more_examples: Get ready, we're leaving in five minutes.
It takes her an hour to get ready.
forms: got ready · getting ready · be ready

real_life.work: "I need to get ready for the meeting."

conversation: B: I get ready in ten minutes.
speaking_task: Describe how you get ready on a work or school morning.

example: I take a shower after my walk.

hindi_example.dev: मैं टहलने के बाद नहाता हूँ।
hindi_example.roman: Main tahalne ke baad nahaata hoon.

gap.q: I ___ a shower after my walk.

not_when: For a bath in a tub ("take a bath").
memory: Take = have; shower = water from above.
simple: To wash your body under a shower.
more_examples: I take a shower every morning.
Let me take a shower first.
forms: took a shower · taking a shower

confusing.pair: take a shower vs take a bath
confusing.diff: Shower = standing; bath = in a tub; Indians often say "bath" for both.

real_life.work: "Let me take a shower after the gym, then join the call."
real_life.casual: "I need to take a shower, I'm so sweaty!"

conversation: B: I take a shower after my walk. Give me ten minutes.
speaking_task: Describe your morning routine with this and two more daily chunks.

when: When you talk about the morning meal
example: We have breakfast at eight.

hindi_example.dev: हम आठ बजे नाश्ता करते हैं।
hindi_example.roman: Hum aath baje naashta karte hain.

gap.q: We ___ breakfast at eight.

simple: To eat the morning meal.

confusing.diff: "Take breakfast" is old Indian English; "have" is natural.

conversation: B: We have breakfast at eight.
speaking_task: Tell someone what you have for breakfast and when.

when: When you talk about sleeping time
example: I go to bed at eleven.

hindi_example.dev: मैं ग्यारह बजे सोने जाता हूँ।
hindi_example.roman: Main gyaarah baje sone jaata hoon.

gap.q: I go to ___ at eleven.

not_when: Don't add "the": not "go to the bed".
simple: To lie down in bed to sleep.
more_examples: I go to bed at eleven.
forms: went to bed · going to bed
similar: go to sleep · hit the sack

confusing.pair: go to bed vs go to sleep
confusing.diff: "Go to bed" = lie down; "go to sleep" = fall asleep.

real_life.work: "I go to bed early before a big day."

conversation: B: I go to bed at eleven.
speaking_task: Describe your night routine.

when: When you talk about schoolwork at home
example: I do my homework after dinner.

hindi_example.dev: मैं खाने के बाद अपना होमवर्क करता हूँ।
hindi_example.roman: Main khaane ke baad apna homework karta hoon.

gap.q: I ___ my homework after dinner. (make / do)

simple: To complete schoolwork at home.
more_examples: I do my homework after school.

confusing.diff: We "do" work and tasks; we "make" things.

real_life.work: "Kids do homework while I work from home."

conversation: B: I do my homework after dinner.
speaking_task: Talk about when and where you do homework or study.

example: Can you take a photo of us?

hindi_example.dev: क्या आप हमारी एक फ़ोटो खींच सकते हैं?
hindi_example.roman: Kya aap hamaari ek photo kheench sakte hain?
